Because of the decisions I handed down in the famous and sulphurous cases of attempted poisoning of the Head of State and of undermining the security of the State, I am persecuted, and my exile has not stopped my pursuers in their base design to kill me, if not physically, then at least socially and professionally.

A communiqué of reprisals

I learned, with a certain bewilderment, that a communiqué of Thursday 22 May 2014, broadcast on a loop on national television, invited me to resume service by 26 May 2014 at the latest, failing which I would be considered to have resigned. Only ridicule is left to finish off certain officials of my country!!!

I do not understand the intellectual deafness of the authors of this communiqué, who must have been on another planet while the whole debate was unfolding on how to ensure my security and that of my family after the handing down of the orders of 17 May 2013. That debate is still current, since no provision has yet been made for me to exercise, freely and in complete peace of mind, my right to remain in my country and to serve it usefully.

I am a magistrate and as such I remain subject to the duty of professional reserve. That is moreover why I have so far refrained from making certain statements useful for enlightening people about the true morality of these cases that I investigated. But for me, the obligation of reserve must not be perceived as a masochistic command turning every magistrate into a Saint Sebastian riddled with arrows. My honour has been publicly attacked and my professional integrity has been called into question. Because these are matters that touch deeply on my dignity, I have decided to use my constitutional right to speak.

I therefore denounce here the blatant machiavellianism of the authors of the communiqué. In truth, it is hardly necessary to recall that they are not unaware that it is perfectly impossible for me to go and resume service on 26 May 2014, and this for two fundamental reasons. First, the conditions of my security are still not clearly met in the country. Indeed, there remains a price on my head from those who felt wronged and thrown off course by my two orders of dismissal. Second, I am involved in an asylum procedure here in the United States. It follows that inviting me to resume service by 26 May 2014 at the latest, without giving any guarantee of my security and disregarding the said procedure, is manifestly insincere and therefore a “non-lieu” (no case to answer). It is proof of a severe apoplexy…

It must be affirmed that the authors of the communiqué are wrong to consider my exile a fiction and to call me back to resume service as if I had gone off on a health outing. I left Benin in the face of the complicit negligence of the competent authorities in protecting me against arbitrariness and the base instincts of a losing and frantic vengeance.

A burlesque communiqué that betrays the renewed desire to push up the daisies on my behalf! For me, this communiqué is a “non-lieu”. One may well wonder what purpose this communiqué of 22 May 2014 serves in this “re-creation”, if not to prolong the reprisals and the indelible scars inflicted on me in order to satisfy who knows what vendetta. If Man were God? I know, and all the Beninese people with me, where this is heading.

Easy to forgive when one has finished taking revenge

I am not against forgiveness. It is a good thing to forgive. Forgiveness “warms the heart and cools the sting” (William Arthur WARD). It allows one to “take back the reins of our destiny and to recognise the other as still capable of reconnecting with good”. François VERILLON said it: forgiveness is “neither a wipe of the sponge nor a wash, but a re-creation”.

Although I am a man of law, I do not wish to question the legal implications of this pardon which, as sensible jurists have analysed, is an exit by break-in that neither empties the substance of the proceedings nor corrects the tarnished image of my country, where inevitably the republican deficit takes precedence over democratic renewal.

Forgiveness raises inexhaustible discussions, namely: What does this pardon conceal? What is its degree of sincerity? In this drama which has so divided the people and shattered whole lives, is it the best thing to do? Why does it come at the precise moment when the Supreme Court has handed down its rulings in these cases? What is to be said of a pardon granted when it was not requested? What is to be said of a pardon intended for persons who benefited from a dismissal of charges? So many questions which indeed invite one to think of this sentence by Josh BILLINGS: “there is no revenge so complete as forgiveness”.

Revenge! That is the fundamental evil which, in this affair, has done more damage than the deadly plots that were supposedly hatched. I am regarded as collateral damage in this affair. This is not a figment of the imagination; I paid the highest price for it. From the day I received these files in my chambers until today, I have never again had a life of my own or lived it to the full.

During the investigation of the cases, I endured all kinds of pressure, in the form of harassment, outrageous surveillance, and systematic intrusion into and occupation of my private life. These cases isolated me from my family, from my relatives. Holed up, paralysed, I no longer had a life, a freedom… from then on at the mercy of shadowers and ill-intentioned informers.

From my upbringing I was able to draw the necessary energy and sufficient courage to do my work and complete it on 17 May 2013. Unsurprisingly, the persecution escalated…

An endless persecution

I was called every name: “corrupt judge”, “steeped in charlatanism”, “leading a loose life”… I endured everything, absorbed everything. With one consolation only: none of my accusers managed to bring proof of their lying allegations, and my decisions were never contradicted, at least legally.

Across the country, people marched against me in whole crowds, threatening me with mob justice. In all the tabernacles of the country, my head was demanded of God and of the gods. A horde of journalists and “hack-writers” was unleashed against me with the base aim of sullying my name forever… Friends and relatives were infiltrated, either to spy on my every move or to bring serious and concordant evidence likely to catch me in the act. Some resisted bravely. Others succumbed in cowardice… When one has lived in such infernal bonds, daily at death’s door, the survival instinct can only be stronger.

Escorted by the invisible protective blessing of the Beninese people, I braved the insecurity apparatus set around me, crossing, on one mild Friday, bush, mud and river at the risk of meeting death at any moment.

On arriving in the United States on 1 December 2013, it was as if I had fallen from the frying pan into the heart of the fire. At John Fitzgerald KENNEDY international airport, I was notified that there was a problem with my visa. For a few minutes, I had the profound feeling of being an ordinary citizen. But very soon I pulled myself together. I had to convince myself that I had, after all, just escaped death and that I was in a country where sensitivity to truth and to human rights is supposed to be the strongest in the world. Yet the doubt lasted eighteen (18) days, during which I knew the pain and the blues of detention. I, who once issued committal warrants against certain defendants at the Cotonou court. The credibility of the fear I invoked having been recognised, I won in this ultra-organised country the right not to be returned to the hell from which I had just escaped. Here, people are more serious and each applies himself to doing his work without bias. It is with great respect and gripped by emotion that I express to them my sincere thanks.

It is this man, persecuted to the utmost for having done his job, who was absent from the recollection of the facts on the day of the outpouring of the presidential pardon. Obviously, I am not asking to be pardoned. For I have done nothing that would justify such an outpouring towards me! I am not detained in this affair. I am forced into exile in the framework of this affair of which I am a perfect victim. One does not forgive a victim. One asks a victim for forgiveness. One offers her apologies and restores her in her inalienable right to live in peace and security in her homeland. The fact of having obscured this in the official discourse of the pardon, and of lashing out in addition with a villainous and facetious communiqué like that of 22 May 2014, is sufficient proof that the work of vengeance is still under way. Easy to forgive when one has finished taking revenge!

Forgiveness, regarded by an Arab proverb as “the most beautiful flower of victory”, manifestly completes the revenge by which the future of so many Beninese has been compromised and by which people like me — who, out of mad passion for the country, could not bear to live a whole week away from their native soil — have been driven into exile.

In the marketing pardon of 14 May 2014, I sense something purely La Rochefoucauldian: administering this pardon is only a sibylline way of asking for forgiveness. I repeat: the pardon does not concern me. For I am involved in none of the cases. I am a judge, in the service of the law. And in law, the facts brought before me do not constitute offences under criminal law. Since 17 May 2013, when I said so in my orders, no other judge has come forward to prove the contrary. No serious jurist has taken the opposite view. My decisions were confirmed on appeal. The Supreme Court did not rule on my orders. It rather quashed the confirmatory rulings of the indictment chamber on a point of form, and this for a simple visa problem. Better still, the decision of the differently composed Indictment Chamber of Monday 19 May 2014, granting provisional release to the accused in these cases, is nothing but a partial execution of the dismissal orders of 17 May 2013.

A firm confidence in the future

Respecting the law, bowing before the law, is not only a mere politeness nor a banal act of wisdom. It is the royal road to giving good governance a chance in our country. And the more I think about it, the more I realise that I am assuming my destiny to the end.

The function of a contemporary judge is very different from what we knew in the past. Nowadays, the judge must avoid isolating himself. He must strive not only to be more and more accessible to the public, but he must also take an interest in the life of his city.

There, then, are so many good reasons to motivate my commitment to live henceforth a more active citizenship based on the exercise of my right to speak and of my duty to contribute to improving the governance of my country. On entering the magistracy, I was concerned to contribute to correcting man and elevating the nation by enforcing the law. But this would be a vain undertaking if politics remains the preserve of people whose tendency to failure is matched only by their gluttony.

I must therefore perfect my function as a goad, as a detonator. When one has grappled with certain flaws, when one has dared to say no to the muzzling of the house of justice, one can no longer simply keep quiet. Any prolonged silence becomes a work of complicity, especially in a public space transformed into an arena where the actors contrive to make the general interest perish for the benefit of their bellies and their pride. As long as politics falls this low, the country will not be able to emerge from the depths of underdevelopment.

As I finish this reflection, a conviction inhabits me. My country, indeed, seems handed over to people without faith or law. Its leaders have renounced their duties, those of working to establish a society of values, of order, of justice and of security. The drama of my country is not so much the venomous influence of these practices as the silence of enlightened consciences and the compromise of the elites. As long as the situation remains thus, the work of development will be a Sisyphean task.

In 2006, we had a formidable project of change and progress. Over the years and the drifts, this miracle project has turned into a sad memorial to the patent failure of the ruling elites. A national shame that must be corrected forthwith at the next opportunity. To remain on the sidelines of this process of renewal would be a crime against the country.

Let the enlightened consciences of all Benin know it and commit themselves. From now on! My country can count on me to play my part fully and without faltering. I am no longer afraid of anything, not even death, for to be killed for a truth that has become so unavoidable as to prompt a pardon would inevitably increase my chances of going to paradise. But it is not about me, it is about the whole of Benin. And we will not let it perish in just any hands!

New York, 26 May 2014
Judge Angelo Djidjoho HOUSSOU

a5707.t:
Italian energy company Eni (ENI.MI), opens new tab is in talks with Japan on supplying the country with liquefied natural gas (LNG), Cristian Signoretto, Eni’s director for global gas and LNG portfolio, told reporters on the sidelines of a conference on Sunday.
“We already deal with Japanese buyers on a short-term basis and we would like to expand that collaboration also to a long-term basis,” Signoretto said, adding that Eni plans to bring more LNG volumes to the market, including from Indonesia and also wants Japanese financial institutions to support some projects.
Eni plans to build its LNG portfolio to 18 million metric tonnes per year by 2027 and would be ready to commit part of it to Japan, if the opportunity is there, he added.
Signoretto, said it was early to say about the specifics of the discussions, including whether Eni would insist on destination clauses, which are obligations in contracts for the buyer not to resell the gas to third parties.
In recent years, there has been a growing demand among Japanese buyers for deals with shorter duration and without destination clauses as this allows buyers in Japan, the world’s second-biggest LNG importer, to stay flexible and also to resell LNG.
“Flexibility will be part of the discussion,” Signoretto said, without providing details.

a5852.t:
US-Hilfen auf dem Prüfstand
Gesundheitsminister versichert Fortführung wichtiger Programme
            
                        Namibia zeigt sich unbeeindruckt von der Aussetzung der US-Entwicklungshilfe. Eine „humanitäre Ausnahmeregelung" stellt sicher, dass lebenswichtige HIV-Medikamente weiterhin verfügbar sind. Laut Gesundheitsministerium seien essenzielle Programme nicht gefährdet.
                        
            
                
            Von Elizabeth Kheibes
(Bearbeitet von Yvonne Jarosch)
Windhoek
Nach der Entscheidung der US-Regierung, Teile ihrer Auslandshilfeprogramme vorübergehend auszusetzen, betont Gesundheitsminister Dr. Kalumbi Shangula, dass wichtige Gesundheitsprogramme weitergeführt werden – auch falls die US-Unterstützung dauerhaft entfällt. Eine humanitäre Ausnahmeregelung stellt zudem sicher, dass Millionen Menschen weiterhin Zugang zu lebensrettenden HIV-Medikamenten haben.
Dr. Kalumbi Shangula begrüßte die Entscheidung des US-Außenministers Marco Rubio, eine „humanitäre Ausnahmeregelung“ zu genehmigen, die sicherstellt, dass Millionen von Menschen weltweit, auch in Namibia, weiterhin eine lebensrettende HIV-Behandlung erhalten. Shangula warnte davor, dass ein Rückzug der amerikanischen Unterstützung verheerende Folgen haben könnte. „Das sollte überhaupt nicht passieren. Fragen, die Menschenleben betreffen, müssen immer gewahrt bleiben“, sagte er. Er vermutet, dass die ursprüngliche Entscheidung möglicherweise nicht ausreichend durchdacht wurde und nun korrigiert werde.
Namibia profitiert erheblich von der Unterstützung durch das US-Programm PEPFAR (United States President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief), das seit seiner Gründung über 20 Milliarden N$ (ca. 1,1 Milliarden US$) in die HIV/AIDS-Bekämpfung des Landes investiert hat. 2022 stellte PEPFAR 1,7 Milliarden N$ bereit, 2023 folgten weitere 840 Millionen N$ über USAID zur Versorgung gefährdeter Gruppen mit Gesundheits- und Sozialdiensten.
Eine Ankündigung des US-Außenministeriums signalisierte eine vorübergehende Aussetzung der Auslandshilfeprogramme – einschließlich derjenigen im Rahmen von PEPFAR – während Donald Trump die internationale Entwicklungshilfe neu bewertet. Der Zugang zu lebenswichtigen HIV-Medikamenten bleibt gewährleistet.
Entscheidung rettet Leben
Die humanitäre Ausnahmeregelung ermöglicht es, dass HIV-Medikamente trotz der laufenden Prüfung der US-Auslandshilfe weiterhin in 55 Ländern verfügbar sind. „UNAIDS begrüßt diese wichtige Entscheidung der US-Regierung, die Millionen Menschen während der Überprüfung der Auslandshilfe den Zugang zu lebensrettenden HIV-Medikamenten garantiert“, sagte UNAIDS-Exekutivdirektorin Winnie Byanyima.
Shangula versicherte der Öffentlichkeit, dass Namibias Gesundheitsprogramme auch bei einem vollständigen Rückzug der US-Hilfe gesichert seien. Die Regierung arbeite kontinuierlich daran, die Nachhaltigkeit der wichtigsten Gesundheitsinitiativen zu gewährleisten. „Alle unsere Programme sind integraler Bestandteil der Kernaktivitäten des Ministeriums“, erklärte er. Seit der Unabhängigkeit habe die Regierung jährlich Betriebs- und Kapitalkosten eingeplant. Internationale Spenden seien wertvoll, aber lediglich ergänzend.
USA setzt teilweise aus
In Simbabwe wurde USAID bereits angewiesen, sämtliche Aktivitäten im Rahmen einer spezifischen Vereinbarung einzustellen, darunter auch Projekte zu Vielfalt, Gerechtigkeit, Inklusion und Zugänglichkeit (DEIA). Organisationen müssen nachweisen, dass DEIA-Aktivitäten ausgesetzt wurden und ihre Kosten minimieren.
Die betroffenen Organisationen wurden zudem aufgefordert, ihre Verträge zu überprüfen und detaillierte Berichte darüber vorzulegen, wie die DEIA-bezogenen Arbeiten eingestellt werden können, während gleichzeitig die Einhaltung der Aussetzungsanordnung sichergestellt wird. In Namibia gibt es bislang keine Hinweise auf unmittelbare Einschränkungen. Selma Shiwaya, Sprecherin von IntraHealth Namibia, erklärte, dass sie sich nicht zu den möglichen Auswirkungen dieser Entscheidung auf ihre Geschäftstätigkeit äußern könne.

a5852.en:
US aid under scrutiny

US aid under scrutiny
Health Minister assures continuation of important programmes

Namibia appears unimpressed by the suspension of US development aid. A "humanitarian exemption" ensures that vital HIV medicines remain available. According to the Health Ministry, essential programmes are not at risk.

By Elizabeth Kheibes
(Edited by Yvonne Jarosch)
Windhoek
Following the US government's decision to temporarily suspend parts of its foreign aid programmes, Health Minister Dr Kalumbi Shangula stresses that important health programmes will be continued - even if US support ceases permanently. A humanitarian exemption also ensures that millions of people continue to have access to life-saving HIV medicines.

Dr Kalumbi Shangula welcomed the decision by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio to approve a "humanitarian exemption" which ensures that millions of people worldwide, including in Namibia, continue to receive life-saving HIV treatment. Shangula warned that a withdrawal of American support could have devastating consequences. "That should not happen at all. Matters that concern human lives must always be preserved," he said. He suspects that the original decision may not have been sufficiently thought through and is now being corrected.

Namibia benefits considerably from support through the US programme PEPFAR (United States President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief), which since its creation has invested more than N$20 billion (about US$1.1 billion) in the country's fight against HIV/AIDS. In 2022 PEPFAR provided N$1.7 billion; in 2023 a further N$840 million followed through USAID to supply vulnerable groups with health and social services.

An announcement by the US State Department signalled a temporary suspension of foreign aid programmes - including those under PEPFAR - while Donald Trump reassesses international development assistance. Access to vital HIV medicines remains guaranteed.

Decision saves lives

The humanitarian exemption makes it possible for HIV medicines to remain available in 55 countries despite the ongoing review of US foreign aid. "UNAIDS welcomes this important decision by the US government, which guarantees millions of people access to life-saving HIV medicines during the review of foreign aid," said UNAIDS Executive Director Winnie Byanyima.

Shangula assured the public that Namibia's health programmes are secure even in the event of a complete withdrawal of US aid. The government is working continuously to ensure the sustainability of the most important health initiatives. "All our programmes are an integral part of the ministry's core activities," he explained. Since independence the government has budgeted annually for operating and capital costs. International donations are valuable, but merely supplementary.

USA partially suspends

In Zimbabwe, USAID has already been instructed to halt all activities under a specific agreement, including projects on diversity, equity, inclusion and accessibility (DEIA). Organisations must demonstrate that DEIA activities have been suspended and minimise their costs.

The organisations concerned were also required to review their contracts and submit detailed reports on how DEIA-related work can be discontinued while at the same time ensuring compliance with the suspension order. In Namibia there are so far no indications of immediate restrictions. Selma Shiwaya, spokeswoman for IntraHealth Namibia, stated that she could not comment on the possible effects of this decision on their operations.

a5853.t:
• Botswana is proving to be USA’ ‘partner of choice’ in the region for its military exercise and operations
                    Botswana is “a steadfast partner of the United States”, the US Ambassador Van Vranken said in his opening remarks at the ongoing US Africa Command (AFRICOM) African Chiefs of Defense Conference 2024 in Gaborone.
Also attending the Conference were US Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Air Force General Charles Q. Brown Jr and Commander of AFRICOM, General Michael E. Langley.
The chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff is the US' highest-ranking military officer and the principal military advisor to the president, the secretary of defense and the National Security Council.
Perhaps in testimony to US-Botswana military relations, Ambassador Van Vranken announced to the Conference that Botswana will soon host AFRICOM’s flagship military exercise; Southern Accord 2024.
The two-week exercise is set to commence on August 5th and end on August 16, 2024. It is set to take place in three locations including Thebephatshwa Air Base, Botswana.
The preparations for Southern Accord 2024, which will be led by U.S. Army Southern European Task Force, Africa (SETAF-AF), are at final stages with joint-planning conference having been concluded on June 21, 2024 in Gaborone.
The exercise is said to cover a variety of operations including humanitarian assistance, disaster relief, peacekeeping and aeromedical evacuation.
It is not the first time Botswana host US military exercise of that magnitude; having hosted Southern Accord in 2012. In 2012, the exercise involved just over battalion strength of the two militaries.
Botswana is proving to be US’ ‘partner of choice’ in the region for its military exercise and operations. In 2019, Botswana hosted AFRICOM’s Operation Upward Minute Man and African Land Forces Summit which brought together over 40 African Land Forces Chiefs.
In the subsequent years, Botswana has gone on to host several Joint Combined Exchange Trainings (JCETS) between BDF and US Special Forces.
In June 2023, Botswana hosted AFRICOM’s Security Implications of Climate Change Symposium which has since been followed by the ongoing conference which has brought together over 30 defence chiefs from the continent
and various subject-matter experts from US and NATO.
In the context of the unravelling geo-strategic environment, particularly in North Africa and the Sahel, it is not surprising that the US is under pressure to pursue other bilateral and multilateral endeavours to counter its perceived strategic adversaries and reaffirm and reassert its waning influence in the continent.
It is the first time the African Chiefs of Defense Conference is held on African soil and the attendance of General Charles Brown, demonstrates US’ desired strategic dividends from the engagement.
The US is faced with strategic ‘repulsion’ in the Sahel and some part of West Africa, as Niger and Tchad have already called for withdrawal of US troops.
The head of Niger's ruling Conseil National pour la sauvegarde de la patrie, (CNSP) or National Council for the Safeguard of the Homeland, Brigadier General Abdourahamane Tiani has given the US up to September 15th, 2024 to have completed withdrawal of troops, as Russia takes the centre-stage.
There are fears that the great power play playing out in some parts of Africa may be slowly creeping into the SADC region. In February 2023, Russia, China, and South Africa conducted maritime exercise, Exercise Mosi-II which as expected, drew condemnation from the US and its allies.

a5864.t:
The Irish government plans to invest 406.8 million meticais (€5.4 million) in social infrastructure projects in the province of Niassa, northern Mozambique, provincial authorities announced yesterday.
According to a note from the Niassa Provincial Executive Council, the funding, which will be implemented up until 2030, will contribute to the construction of boarding schools, solar-powered water supply systems, a maternal and child health unit, as well as irrigation and processing systems “to improve the agricultural value chain”, among others.
“Our partnership goes beyond financing; it is about contributing to the promotion of sustainable development and the construction of a dignified future,” said Edgar Ussene, representative of the Irish Embassy in Niassa, quoted in the document.
For Celestina Teófilo, director of the provincial governor’s office, also cited in the note, Irish funding places the population at the centre of priorities, “guaranteeing sustainable results” for the province’s development.
In 2022, Ireland made available more than 16 million meticais (€212,700) for humanitarian assistance to those displaced by terrorism in Niassa province. In addition, Ireland pledged more than US$700,000 (€594,000) to support social projects in the province.

a6038.t:
Les derniers développements dans la presse ouest-africaine révèlent des tensions tant sur le plan politique qu’économique, allant des rivalités électorales en Côte d’Ivoire aux difficultés budgétaires du Sénégal, en passant par l’inflation au Bénin, a constaté mercredi APA.
Bénin Web TV rapporte une « légère hausse des prix en janvier 2025 » dans le pays, précisant que l’Indice harmonisé des prix à la consommation (IHPC) a atteint 100,7 en janvier 2025 contre 100,4 en décembre 2024, soit une augmentation de 0,3 %. Cette progression est principalement attribuée à la hausse des prix des produits alimentaires et des transports.
En Côte d’Ivoire, Financial Afrik souligne que Tidjane Thiam fait face à une situation de « l’Ivoirité », se demandant si un scénario similaire à celui de Barack Obama pourrait se produire en Afrique. Bien que l’investiture de Tidjane Thiam comme candidat du Parti démocratique de Côte d’Ivoire-Rassemblement démocratique africain (PDCI-RDA, fondé par son oncle Félix Houphouët-Boigny, père de la Nation) semblait assurée pour l’élection présidentielle d’octobre 2025, il se retrouve soudainement sous le feu des critiques, y compris au sein de son propre camp, indique le site d’informations.
À l’approche de la présidentielle prévue en octobre prochain, Jeune Afrique rapporte que l’ex-président Laurent Gbagbo est engagé dans une « lutte perpétuelle », semblant être un « goût d’inachevé ». A 80 ans cette année, l’ancien président a entamé un nouveau combat : celui de sa réinscription sur les listes électorales ivoiriennes en vue de se présenter à l’élection présidentielle. Il a récemment lancé une tournée de mobilisation, souligne le magazine.
Malgré ces tensions politiques, le Premier Ministre Robert Beugré a salué l’esprit de dialogue social des syndicalistes, rapporte Abidjan.net. La 15e édition du Forum de la rentrée syndicale de la Confédération syndicale internationale (CSI)-Afrique s’est ouverte ce mardi 25 février 2025 à Grand-Bassam, sous la présidence de Robert Beugré Mambé, Premier Ministre, Ministre des Sports et du Cadre de vie. Dans son allocution, le Chef du gouvernement a encouragé les syndicalistes à poursuivre leur engagement dans un dialogue social constructif, gage de progrès économique et social, a précisé le média ivoirien.
Au Sénégal, Le Monde Afrique souligne les difficultés du gouvernement face à la gestion des comptes publics, indiquant que la dette du pays atteint 99,67 % du PIB et le déficit budgétaire 12,3 %, selon la Cour des comptes. Le gouvernement assure qu’il ne recourra pas à une cure d’austérité.
Walf Quotidien rapporte également que le secteur du BTP est « sous tension », confronté à une dette intérieure, des créances bancaires, des problèmes fiscaux et une trésorerie difficile. Le quotidien sénégalais ajoute que la situation semble préoccupante pour les industries agroalimentaires en raison de la deuxième baisse annoncée des prix des produits de première nécessité.
Concernant la suspension de l’agence gouvernementale américaine d’aide (USAID), le journal note que l’ancien président Macky Sall « minimise la mesure » prise par Donald Trump. « L’Afrique n’est plus dans une perspective de tendre la main », a-t-il affirmé dans L’AS.
ODL/ac/Sf/APA
a6038.en:
The latest developments in the West African press reveal tensions on both the political and the economic front, ranging from electoral rivalries in Côte d'Ivoire to Senegal's budgetary difficulties, by way of inflation in Benin, APA observed on Wednesday.

Bénin Web TV reports a "slight rise in prices in January 2025" in the country, specifying that the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP) reached 100.7 in January 2025 against 100.4 in December 2024, an increase of 0.3%. This rise is mainly attributed to the increase in the prices of food products and of transport.

In Côte d'Ivoire, Financial Afrik points out that Tidjane Thiam is facing a situation of "Ivoirité", wondering whether a scenario similar to that of Barack Obama could occur in Africa. Although Tidjane Thiam's investiture as the candidate of the Democratic Party of Côte d'Ivoire–African Democratic Rally (PDCI-RDA, founded by his uncle Félix Houphouët-Boigny, father of the Nation) seemed assured for the presidential election of October 2025, he suddenly finds himself under fire from critics, including within his own camp, the news site indicates.

As the presidential election scheduled for next October approaches, Jeune Afrique reports that former president Laurent Gbagbo is engaged in a "perpetual struggle", seeming to have a "taste of the unfinished". At 80 years old this year, the former president has begun a new fight: that of his re-registration on the Ivorian electoral rolls with a view to standing in the presidential election. He recently launched a mobilisation tour, the magazine stresses.

Despite these political tensions, Prime Minister Robert Beugré praised the trade unionists' spirit of social dialogue, Abidjan.net reports. The 15th edition of the Forum of the Trade Union New Year of the International Trade Union Confederation (ITUC)-Africa opened on Tuesday 25 February 2025 at Grand-Bassam, under the chairmanship of Robert Beugré Mambé, Prime Minister, Minister of Sports and of the Living Environment. In his address, the head of government encouraged trade unionists to continue their engagement in constructive social dialogue, a guarantee of economic and social progress, the Ivorian media outlet specified.

In Senegal, Le Monde Afrique highlights the government's difficulties in managing the public accounts, indicating that the country's debt has reached 99.67% of GDP and the budget deficit 12.3%, according to the Court of Auditors. The government assures that it will not resort to a course of austerity.

Walf Quotidien also reports that the construction and public works sector is "under tension", confronted with domestic debt, bank claims, tax problems and difficult cash flow. The Senegalese daily adds that the situation appears worrying for the agri-food industries because of the second announced reduction in the prices of basic necessities.

Concerning the suspension of the American government aid agency (USAID), the paper notes that former president Macky Sall "plays down the measure" taken by Donald Trump. "Africa is no longer in a perspective of holding out its hand," he stated in L'AS.

ODL/ac/Sf/APA

a6096.t:
US President Donald Trump has called for the chair of the Federal Reserve to quit right away, in an escalation of his attacks on Jerome Powell.
"'Too Late' should resign immediately!!!", Trump said in a post on his Truth Social platform.
He also included a link to a news article about a US federal housing regulator calling for Mr Powell to be investigated over his testimony about renovations to the central bank's Washington headquarters.
Trump nominated Mr Powell to be the Fed chair during his first term. Since then, he has repeatedly criticised him for not cutting interest rates but it is unclear whether the president has the authority to remove him from the post.
Despite the president's continued criticism of Mr Powell, he said earlier this year that had "no intention of firing him".
Trump wants the Federal Reserve to lower interest rates to help boost economic growth.
Mr Powell said on Tuesday that the Fed would have cut rates already had it not been for the impact of Trump's tariff policies.
When asked during a meeting of central bankers in Portugal whether US rates would have been cut again this year if the administration had not announced its plan to sharply increase tariffs on countries around the world Mr Powell responded, "I think that's right."
The US Federal Reserve declined to comment about Trump's remarks when contacted by the BBC.
Mr Powell was renominated to the position by then-President Joe Biden and his current term is set to end in May 2026.
Ahead of Trump's return to power at the start of this year, Mr Powell said he would not step down if the president asked him to and that it is "not permitted under law" for the White House to force him out.
Board members of independent federal agencies like the Federal Reserve can only be forced out before their terms expire "for cause," according to a landmark US Supreme Court ruling in 1935.
However, Trump has often challenged political norms, including firing some independent regulators, actions that have been contested in court.
On Wednesday, Federal Housing Finance Agency director Bill Pulte, who has previously strongly criticised Mr Powell, called for him to be investigated.
"I am asking Congress to investigate Chairman Jerome Powell, his political bias, and his deceptive Senate testimony, which is enough to be removed 'for cause'," he posted on X.
Last week, Mr Powell told the Senate that reports about soaring costs and expensive features at the Fed's headquarters were "misleading and inaccurate in many, many respects."

a6135.t:
Après des mois de blocage, un navire humanitaire affrété par l’ONU a quitté le port de Pivdenny, dans le sud de l’Ukraine, avec 23.000 tonnes de blé à son bord, a annoncé le ministère ukrainien de l’Infrastructure. « Le navire Brave Commander avec du grain pour l’Afrique a quitté le port de Pivdenny. Ce matin, le cargo est parti pour le port de Djibouti, où les vivres seront livrées à l’arrivée aux consommateurs en Ethiopie », a indiqué le ministère sur Telegram. Ce premier chargement, dont l’arrivée est attendue à Djibouti le 25 août prochain d’après les informations transmises par Marine Traffic, est « une étape importante pour la réintégration de la production alimentaire ukrainienne dans le marché alimentaire mondial et permet de venir en aide à des pays frappés par d’importantes pénuries alimentaires via des couloirs commerciaux et humanitaires », a déclaré le Programme alimentaire mondial (PAM).
Présent au port de Pivdenny dimanche, le ministre ukrainien de l’Infrastructure Oleksandre Koubrakov avait dit espérer que « deux ou trois » navires supplémentaires affrétés par l’ONU pourraient en partir prochainement.
Pour sa part, l’Agence américaine d’aide au développement (USAID) a précisé dans un communiqué mardi avoir fourni 68 millions de dollars au Programme alimentaire mondial de l’ONU (PAM) pour l’achat, le transport et le stockage de 150 000 tonnes de blé ukrainien.
« L’USAID […] a soutenu le premier envoi humanitaire de céréales à quitter la mer noire via le port ukrainien de Yuzhny aujourd’hui », indique le communiqué de l’agence qui précise qu’avant la guerre, l’Ukraine était l’un des principaux fournisseurs de céréales du PAM. Il s’agit de la première cargaison d’aide alimentaire à quitter l’Ukraine depuis qu’ont été signés en juillet par Kiev et Moscou, via une médiation de la Turquie et sous l’égide de l’ONU, des accords sur l’exportation des céréales ukrainiennes, bloquées à cause de la guerre entre les deux pays. Selon les Nations Unies, entre le 1er et le 15 août, 11 vraquiers ont été autorisés à quitter Odessa, 6 Tchornomorsk et 4 Pivdenny. Ces 21 navires transportaient, au total, 563 317 tonnes de matières premières agricoles dont 451 481 tonnes de maïs. Les principaux destinataires de ces livraisons ont été la Turquie (26 % des volumes), l’Iran (22 %) et la Corée du Sud (22 %).
a6135.en:
After months of blockage, a humanitarian vessel chartered by the UN has left the port of Pivdenny, in southern Ukraine, carrying 23,000 tonnes of wheat, the Ukrainian Ministry of Infrastructure announced. "The vessel Brave Commander with grain for Africa has left the port of Pivdenny. This morning, the cargo ship departed for the port of Djibouti, where the food will be delivered on arrival to consumers in Ethiopia," the ministry indicated on Telegram. This first shipment, whose arrival in Djibouti is expected on 25 August according to information transmitted by Marine Traffic, is "an important step for the reintegration of Ukrainian food production into the global food market and makes it possible to assist countries hit by major food shortages via commercial and humanitarian corridors," the World Food Programme (WFP) declared.

Present at the port of Pivdenny on Sunday, the Ukrainian Infrastructure Minister Oleksandr Kubrakov had said he hoped that "two or three" additional vessels chartered by the UN could leave from there soon.

For its part, the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) specified in a statement on Tuesday that it had provided 68 million dollars to the UN World Food Programme (WFP) for the purchase, transport and storage of 150,000 tonnes of Ukrainian wheat.

"USAID [...] supported the first humanitarian shipment of grain to leave the Black Sea via the Ukrainian port of Yuzhny today," the agency's statement indicates, specifying that before the war Ukraine was one of the WFP's main suppliers of grain. This is the first cargo of food aid to leave Ukraine since agreements on the export of Ukrainian grain, blocked because of the war between the two countries, were signed in July by Kyiv and Moscow, through Turkish mediation and under UN auspices. According to the United Nations, between 1 and 15 August, 11 bulk carriers were authorised to leave Odesa, 6 Chornomorsk and 4 Pivdenny. These 21 vessels carried, in total, 563,317 tonnes of agricultural raw materials, including 451,481 tonnes of maize. The main recipients of these deliveries were Turkey (26% of volumes), Iran (22%) and South Korea (22%).

a6186.t:
Cet appui est destiné à construire la ligne ferroviaire Tanzanie-Burundi, elle est longue de 651 km. Les travaux consisteront en l’aménagement d’une voie unique électrifiée à écartement standard.
Ils seront subdivisés en trois lots : les tronçons Tabora–Kigoma avec 411 km et Uvinza–Maragarazi avec 156 km en Tanzanie ; et le tronçon Maragarazi–Musongati de 84 km au Burundi.
Ce réseau de chemin de fer à écartement standard sera relié à celui de la Tanzanie, donnant accès au port de Dar es Salaam. Au total, 400 km de rails ont été déjà posés en Tanzanie, de Dar es Salaam à Dodoma, depuis le début de la première phase du projet. Le reste du tronçon entre Dodoma et Tabora est en cours de construction.
Le Groupe de la Banque fournira 98,62 millions de dollars au Burundi sous forme de dons et 597,79 millions de dollars à la Tanzanie sous forme de prêts et de garanties pour réaliser ce projet.
La BAD sert de chef de file pour structurer et mobiliser environ 3,2 milliards de dollars auprès d’investisseurs institutionnels, d’agences de crédit à l’exportation, d’institutions financières de développement et de banques commerciales. Le coût total du projet en Tanzanie et au Burundi est estimé à près de 3,93 milliards de dollars.
Selon un communiqué de la BAD, l’accès à un service efficace et rentable de transport en vrac sur de longues distances grâce à la voie unique électrifiée à écartement standard encouragera l’exploitation minière à grande échelle et l’agriculture commerciale.
D’après ce communiqué, ce chemin de fer va transformer le corridor de transport central en un corridor économique en améliorant les opportunités commerciales et manufacturières le long de la zone d’influence du corridor.
« Ce chemin de fer permettra l’exploitation du nickel »
Cette ligne permettra d’abandonner le transport routier par camion, qui est à l’origine d’accidents et de coûts élevés d’entretien des routes. Le réseau ferroviaire débloquera et reliera les principales zones de traitement économique, les parcs industriels, les dépôts intérieurs de conteneurs et les centres urbains le long du corridor central.
Ce qui va améliorer l’accessibilité et de promouvoir les activités économiques. Ce projet contribuera à renforcer la résilience en soutenant la création et le développement d’institutions qui géreront le nouveau secteur ferroviaire au Burundi et en soutenant le renforcement des capacités par le biais de la formation professionnelle dans les deux pays.
Le projet constitue une priorité non seulement dans le cadre du plan directeur ferroviaire de la Communauté de l’Afrique de l’Est (CAE), mais aussi au titre du Programme pour le développement des infrastructures en Afrique (PIDA) de l’Union africaine. Il facilitera la transformation économique et sociale dans les deux pays et dans la région.
La construction de ce chemin de fer permettra au Burundi d’intensifier l’exploitation de son nickel, dont le pays dispose du 10ème plus grand gisement mondial dans les champs miniers de Musongati.
Le pays dispose également de ressources telles que le lithium et le cobalt, qui devraient générer des revenus importants pour le pays grâce à la liaison ferroviaire avec le port de Dar es Salaam qui représente actuellement 80% du commerce d’importation et d’exportation du Burundi.
Cela ajoutera de la valeur au PIB national et permettra au Burundi de disposer de ressources supplémentaires pour accélérer son développement social et économique.
Le projet est aligné sur la Stratégie décennale de la Banque et deux de ses priorités opérationnelles, les « High 5 », « Intégrer l’Afrique » et « Industrialiser l’Afrique ».
Il cadre aussi avec le Document de stratégie d’intégration régionale de la Banque pour l’Afrique de l’Est (2023-2027) et les Documents de stratégie pays (DSP) de la Banque pour la Tanzanie (2021-2025) et le Burundi (2019-2023).
a6186.en:
Burundi-Tanzania-DRC railway, the AfDB releases nearly 700 million dollars

This support is intended to build the Tanzania-Burundi railway line, which is 651 km long. The works will consist of the construction of a single electrified standard-gauge track.

They will be divided into three lots: the Tabora-Kigoma sections with 411 km and Uvinza-Maragarazi with 156 km in Tanzania; and the Maragarazi-Musongati section of 84 km in Burundi.

This standard-gauge railway network will be connected to that of Tanzania, giving access to the port of Dar es Salaam. In total, 400 km of rails have already been laid in Tanzania, from Dar es Salaam to Dodoma, since the start of the first phase of the project. The rest of the section between Dodoma and Tabora is under construction.

The Bank Group will provide 98.62 million dollars to Burundi in the form of grants and 597.79 million dollars to Tanzania in the form of loans and guarantees to carry out this project.

The AfDB is acting as lead arranger to structure and mobilise around 3.2 billion dollars from institutional investors, export credit agencies, development finance institutions and commercial banks. The total cost of the project in Tanzania and Burundi is estimated at nearly 3.93 billion dollars.

According to an AfDB press release, access to an efficient and cost-effective long-distance bulk transport service thanks to the single electrified standard-gauge track will encourage large-scale mining and commercial agriculture.

According to this press release, this railway will transform the central transport corridor into an economic corridor by improving commercial and manufacturing opportunities along the corridor's area of influence.

"This railway will enable the exploitation of nickel"

This line will make it possible to abandon road transport by truck, which is the cause of accidents and high road maintenance costs. The rail network will unlock and connect the main economic processing zones, industrial parks, inland container depots and urban centres along the central corridor.

This will improve accessibility and promote economic activities. This project will help strengthen resilience by supporting the creation and development of institutions that will manage the new railway sector in Burundi and by supporting capacity building through vocational training in both countries.

The project is a priority not only within the framework of the East African Community (EAC) railway master plan, but also under the African Union's Programme for Infrastructure Development in Africa (PIDA). It will facilitate economic and social transformation in both countries and in the region.

The construction of this railway will allow Burundi to intensify the exploitation of its nickel, of which the country has the world's 10th largest deposit in the Musongati mining fields.

The country also has resources such as lithium and cobalt, which should generate significant revenues for the country thanks to the rail link with the port of Dar es Salaam, which currently represents 80% of Burundi's import and export trade.

This will add value to national GDP and will allow Burundi to have additional resources to accelerate its social and economic development.

The project is aligned with the Bank's Ten-Year Strategy and two of its operational priorities, the "High 5s", "Integrate Africa" and "Industrialise Africa".

It also fits with the Bank's Regional Integration Strategy Paper for East Africa (2023-2027) and the Bank's Country Strategy Papers (CSPs) for Tanzania (2021-2025) and Burundi (2019-2023).

a6289.t:
Le Programme alimentaire mondial (PAM) a salué, ce vendredi, un don exceptionnel en faveur des réfugiés, de 23 268 tonnes de riz offert, par le ministère sud-coréen de l’Agriculture, de l’Alimentation et des Affaires rurales (MAFRA). Il s’agit de la plus importante contribution sud-coréenne depuis le début de son soutien aux réfugiés au Kenya en 2018.
Le don de riz par la Corée du Sud, d’une valeur de 18 millions de dollars, permettra de couvrir pendant six mois les besoins alimentaires de 720 000 réfugiés vivant dans les camps de Dadaab, Kakuma et le site de Kalobeyei, à un moment où les ressources humanitaires s’amenuisent.
« Cette contribution généreuse est vitale alors que le nombre de réfugiés au Kenya continue d’augmenter », a déclaré Baimankay Sankoh, directeur pays adjoint du PAM. Ajoutant : « La majorité dépend entièrement de l’aide humanitaire. Ce soutien arrive à point nommé. »
Le nombre de réfugiés et demandeurs d’asile dans le pays a bondi de plus de 70 % en cinq ans, atteignant 843 000 personnes, principalement à cause des crises en Somalie et au Soudan du Sud. Malgré l’appui de plusieurs partenaires, le PAM a été contraint de réduire les rations à un tiers de la quantité normale faute de financement.
Le riz sud-coréen, reconnu pour sa qualité, est livré chaque année selon un calendrier régulier, permettant au PAM d’anticiper ses opérations et d’assurer une aide alimentaire stable.
« La République de Corée est fière de contribuer à atténuer la crise de la faim dans la région », a déclaré Kang Hyung-shik, ambassadeur de Corée du Sud au Kenya.
« Notre engagement humanitaire repose sur une tradition de solidarité internationale », a-t-il poursuivi.
Depuis 2018, la Corée du Sud a fourni au PAM plus de 88 millions de dollars en riz pour soutenir les réfugiés installés au Kenya.
WN/as/lb/te/Sf/APA
a6289.en:
The World Food Programme (WFP) on Friday welcomed an exceptional donation for refugees: 23,268 tonnes of rice offered by the South Korean Ministry of Agriculture, Food and Rural Affairs (MAFRA). It is the largest South Korean contribution since it began supporting refugees in Kenya in 2018.

The rice donation from South Korea, worth $18 million, will cover for six months the food needs of 720,000 refugees living in the Dadaab and Kakuma camps and the Kalobeyei settlement, at a time when humanitarian resources are dwindling.

"This generous contribution is vital as the number of refugees in Kenya continues to grow," said Baimankay Sankoh, WFP deputy country director. He added: "The majority depend entirely on humanitarian aid. This support comes at just the right time."

The number of refugees and asylum seekers in the country has jumped by more than 70% in five years, reaching 843,000 people, mainly because of the crises in Somalia and South Sudan. Despite the support of several partners, WFP has been forced to cut rations to one third of the normal quantity for lack of funding.

South Korean rice, recognised for its quality, is delivered each year on a regular schedule, allowing WFP to plan its operations ahead and to ensure stable food assistance.

"The Republic of Korea is proud to contribute to alleviating the hunger crisis in the region," said Kang Hyung-shik, South Korea's ambassador to Kenya. "Our humanitarian commitment rests on a tradition of international solidarity," he continued.

Since 2018, South Korea has provided WFP with more than $88 million in rice to support refugees settled in Kenya.

WN/as/lb/te/Sf/APA

a6291.t:
……Our minerals power other economies; this paradox must end
The Minister of Solid Minerals Development and Chairman of the African Minerals Strategy Group (AMSG), Dr. Dele Alake, has called for a bold new vision to make minerals the fulcrum of Africa’s transformative industrialization.
“Africa’s minerals have powered industrialization elsewhere while our own economies remain under-industrialized. This paradox must end. Our vision must be clear: to move from extractive dependence to transformative industrialization,” Dr. Alake declared in a statement issued on Sunday the October 5, 2025, in Abuja by Mr. Segun Tomori, anipr, FSCA Special Assistant on Media, to the Honourable Minister of Solid Minerals Development.
Delivering the keynote address at the African Mining Week in Cape Town, South Africa, themed “Vision & Strategy Setting the Stage for Minerals Industrialization,” the minister emphasized that Africa must no longer be content as a supplier of raw minerals but must become a global hub for mineral processing, innovation, and green industrialization.
He noted that the continent is blessed with some of the world’s richest mineral deposits, key to clean energy, digital technologies, advanced manufacturing, and global security.
“Our youth should no longer seek jobs abroad while opportunities lie buried beneath their feet. The time to industrialize is now. Let us set the stage for an Africa that is not just a participant in the global minerals economy, but a driver of its future,” Alake asserted.
Highlighting Nigeria’s ongoing reforms in the mining sector, Alake, represented by the Permanent Secretary, Dr. Farouk Yabo, said the nation is incentivizing local beneficiation from gold refining to lithium processing, revoking dormant licenses to encourage serious investment, and strengthening transparency to attract credible global partners.
He added that Nigeria is also developing a National Critical Minerals Strategy and investing in digital systems for data accessibility and mineral traceability.
Speaking at the Ministerial Roundtable of the African Minerals Strategy Group (AMSG) on the sidelines of the event, Alake reiterated Nigeria’s commitment to creating a $1 trillion economy by 2030 through solid minerals development.
“We are investing in digitizing mining processes from data accessibility to mineral traceability. We are also focusing on bequeathing strong institutions and the right policies to drive reforms. Hence, the ongoing efforts to amend the 2007 Minerals and Mining Act to provide a more robust legislative framework that will propel investments in the mining sector,” he stated.
He emphasized that Nigeria’s minerals will henceforth be traceable, originating only from licensed operators or formalized artisanal and small-scale miners.
Echoing sentiments shared by the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), Alake urged African nations to prioritize mapping their mineral resources to understand their true potential.
“After national mapping, it is the duty of countries to ensure only licensed operators are mining. We must also build adequate capacity for effective supervision,” he said.
During the Country Spotlight Session, Nigeria’s Permanent Secretary presented investment opportunities in the solid minerals sector, showcasing reforms, incentives, and a synopsis of the nation’s mineral endowments.
The African Mining Week brought together ministers from DRC, Zimbabwe, Sierra Leone, and representatives from Nigeria, Gambia, and Ghana, alongside major private-sector players across the continent.

a6311.t:
By Cathy Maulidi:
State Vice President Michael Usi has hailed the United States Agency for International Development (USaid)-funded five year Titukulane Project, describing it as a landmark initiative that has resulted in the sprouting of resilient communities across Malawi.
Usi made the remarks on Tuesday at the Project’s Close-out Learning Event, which marked the closeout of contributions of the project.
Care Malawi and partners were implementing it.
He said the project had demonstrated that when stakeholders join hands, they can move mountains.
- Advertisement -
“The name Titukulane, meaning ‘let’s develop together’, is a fitting testament to what this initiative has stood for; [that is], a hallmark of collaboration, resilience and shared purpose.
“Today, we celebrate not just the closeout of a five-year journey but the legacy of resilience, hope and self-actualisation. This is what Titukulane Project is leaving behind for the communities of Zomba, Mangochi and beyond,” Usi said.
The Vice President said the project was the first of its kind, adding that it was designed around the National Resilience Strategy (NRS of 2018 to 2030)—coordinated through the Department of Disaster Management Affairs—which aimed to shift from a reactive cycle of disaster response to a proactive approach of risk management, preparedness and resilience building.
“This shift is no small feat. For years, Malawi has been at the mercy of climate shocks, from floods and droughts to devastating cyclones that have exacerbated hunger across the country. Yet, with initiatives like the Titukulane Project, we are proving that vulnerability is not our destiny.
- Advertisement -
- Advertisement -
“By embedding climate-smart agricultural practices, diverse livelihood packages, community-driven disaster risk management and inclusive governance mechanisms, the project has shown us that resilience is achievable and sustainable,” Usi said.
Usi said he was elated that the project had empowered community members not only to recover from shocks but
to build stronger systems to withstand future ones.
“I am greatly impressed with the figures from the project, impacting a total of 613,826 individuals with interventions in agriculture, irrigation, livestock, marketing, youth vocational skills development, Wash [water, sanitation and hygiene] and nutrition, including improving coordination of NRS interventions at national and district levels. Malawi can only develop if investments are channeled into building resilient systems,” he said.
He further hailed the project’s alignment with the Malawi (MW) 2063 vision, saying this was another milestone worth celebrating.
“Under MW2063, we envision an inclusive, self-reliant and industrialised middle-income nation. The Titukulane Project has contributed meaningfully to two pillars of this vision,” Usi said.
Project implementer Care Malawi, through its country director Pamela Kuwali, also hailed the project’s successes.
“The Titukulane Project has exemplified the power of collaboration, focusing on three key areas: increasing diversified incomes, improving nutritional status and enhancing institutional capacities.
“This approach has ensured women are at the forefront of our efforts. Notable achievements included empowering communities economically through village savings and loans associations,” she said.
Chief of Party for Titukulane Resilience Food Security Activity Jones Chimpukuso said despite registering successes, there were challenges including the slow start of the project due to the Covid pandemic in 2020-21.
“Major hurdles included tropical cyclones Gombe and Tropical Freddy, cholera, and, most recently, El Niño,” he said.
The five-year Resilience Food Security initiative, which USaid was funding, was implemented by Care International Malawi in partnership with Emmanuel International, IFPRI, National Smallholder Farmers Association of Malawi, Save the Children, and WaterAid.
The project targeted Zomba and Mangochi districts with the primary goal of achieving sustainable, equitable and resilient food and nutrition security for ultra-poor and chronically vulnerable households.

a6450.t:
The House of Representatives on Tuesday resolved to investigate the utilisation of over $4.6 billion in health grants and assistance received by Nigeria from the Global Fund and the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) between 2021 and 2025,.
The resolution followed the adoption of a motion of urgent national importance moved by Philip Agbese (APC, Benue), the deputy spokesperson of the House, during plenary.
The motion came as a result of concerns over Nigeria’s persistent poor health outcomes despite the huge financial inflows
The country’s health system has long faced scrutiny over the management of donor funds.
Despite being among the largest recipients of Global Fund and USAID assistance in Africa, reports continue to highlight weak accountability frameworks, fund leakages, and delays in programme implementation.
Presenting the motion, Mr Agbese noted that Nigeria received an estimated $1.8 billion from the Global Fund between 2021 and 2025 to fight HIV, tuberculosis (TB), and malaria, in addition to $2.8 billion in health assistance from USAID covering various health threats such as HIV, malaria, polio, and tuberculosis between 2022 and 2024.
He added that the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria, established in 2002, was created to accelerate global efforts to end these epidemics, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa, through pooled financing and partnerships.
Mr Agbese further stated that Nigeria has also benefited from over $6 billion in assistance from the U.S. President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR) between 2021 and 2025 for HIV/AIDS control and strengthening health systems across the country.
“Nigeria also received over $6 billion dollars in health assistance from the US President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief from 2021 to 2025 to fight HIV/AIDS and build capacity of Health and community Systems,” he said.
The lawmaker expressed concern that despite these significant interventions, Nigeria continues to bear one of the highest global burdens of HIV, tuberculosis, and malaria.
According to the data he cited, in 2023 alone, about 15,000 children (aged 0–14 years) died from AIDS-related causes in Nigeria, while 51,000 AIDS-related deaths were recorded nationwide, placing Nigeria third globally in HIV deaths and with the highest number of HIV cases in West and Central Africa.
In tuberculosis, Mr Agbese noted that Nigeria ranks first in Africa and sixth in the world, accounting for 4.6 per cent of the global TB burden, while in malaria, the country bears the highest burden worldwide, representing 26.6 per cent of global cases and 31 per cent of global malaria deaths.
He expressed worry that the alarming statistics raise questions about the transparency, coordination, and impact of the grants, especially given that the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare is responsible for implementing USAID-funded projects, while the Country Coordinating Mechanism (CCM) Nigeria oversees Global Fund programmes.
Mr Agbese lamented that there has not been a coordinated and robust oversight by the National Assembly on the utilisation of these grants, despite its constitutional powers under Sections 88 and 89 of the Constitution to summon officials and demand accountability from ministries, agencies, and even non-governmental implementers.
He warned that unless urgent steps are taken to reevaluate and reassess how the grants have been implemented, especially as the Global Fund prepares its 8th Replenishment phase, Nigeria risks failing to meet the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) target of eliminating HIV, TB, and malaria by 2030.
House resolution
Without debate, the House mandated its Committee on HIV/AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria Control to investigate the utilisation of the grants received by Nigeria between 2021 and 2025 for the fight against HIV, TB, and malaria.
The committee was directed to report back to the House within four weeks for further legislative action.
The House also resolved to mandate the Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare to provide details of the implementation plan and National Assembly approvals for the utilisation and expenditure of the grants.

a6492.t:
Le Bureau de la coordination des affaires humanitaires des Nations Unies (OCHA) a exprimé de vives inquiétudes face à la détérioration simultanée de la situation sanitaire et alimentaire au Soudan, en proie à une guerre civile depuis plus de deux ans, a appris mercredi APA.
Au Soudan, pays d’Afrique de l’Est, des millions de personnes déplacées subissent une insécurité alimentaire aiguë et une épidémie de choléra en expansion. Dans l’Etat du Darfour du Nord, particulièrement touché, la localité de Tawila a enregistré depuis juin plus de 1 500 cas suspects et confirmés de choléra, dont 500 malades actuellement sous traitement. Les autorités locales ont instauré des mesures d’urgence, telles que la fermeture des marchés et l’interdiction des rassemblements publics, pour contenir l’épidémie.
Selon le porte-parole adjoint du Secrétaire général de l’ONU, Farhan Haq, « près de 60 % des familles déplacées ne disposent toujours pas d’un abri adéquat » malgré l’aide humanitaire apportée par l’ONU et ses partenaires. Dans le camp d’Abu Shouk, à El Fasher, capitale du Darfour du Nord, des cas de famine ont déjà causé quatre décès la semaine dernière.
Le déficit prolongé en céréales, les mauvaises récoltes et la baisse de l’offre alimentaire font grimper les prix des denrées à des niveaux records. En mai, le coût moyen du panier alimentaire local à El Fasher était plus de six fois supérieur à la moyenne nationale.
L’OCHA estime avoir besoin de 120 millions de dollars pour intensifier son aide humanitaire à Tawila au cours des trois prochains mois. Cette enveloppe est jugée essentielle pour contenir l’épidémie et maintenir les services de base.
Parallèlement, à Port-Soudan, principal point d’entrée du personnel et des fournitures humanitaires, les températures extrêmes et les coupures prolongées d’électricité provoquent une hausse des cas de coups de chaleur, avec un décès signalé ces deux derniers jours.
Le système de classification intégrée de la sécurité alimentaire (IPC) a identifié des conditions de famine dans plusieurs zones du Darfour du Nord et de l’est des montagnes Nuba, avertissant que la situation devrait encore s’aggraver durant la saison maigre, de juillet à octobre, dans les zones de conflit où l’accès humanitaire demeure limité.
ODL/ac/Sf/APA
a6492.en:
The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) has expressed deep concern at the simultaneous deterioration of the health and food situation in Sudan, a country gripped by civil war for more than two years, APA learned on Wednesday.

In Sudan, an East African country, millions of displaced people are suffering acute food insecurity and an expanding cholera epidemic. In North Darfur State, which is particularly hard hit, the locality of Tawila has recorded more than 1,500 suspected and confirmed cases of cholera since June, of whom 500 patients are currently under treatment. Local authorities have introduced emergency measures, such as closing markets and banning public gatherings, to contain the epidemic.

According to the deputy spokesperson for the UN Secretary-General, Farhan Haq, "nearly 60% of displaced families still do not have adequate shelter" despite the humanitarian aid provided by the UN and its partners. In the Abu Shouk camp, in El Fasher, the capital of North Darfur, cases of starvation have already caused four deaths in the past week.

The prolonged cereal deficit, poor harvests and the fall in food supply are driving the prices of foodstuffs to record levels. In May, the average cost of the local food basket in El Fasher was more than six times higher than the national average.

OCHA estimates that it needs 120 million dollars to scale up its humanitarian aid in Tawila over the next three months. This funding is considered essential to contain the epidemic and to maintain basic services.

At the same time, in Port Sudan, the main entry point for humanitarian personnel and supplies, extreme temperatures and prolonged power cuts are causing a rise in cases of heatstroke, with one death reported over the past two days.

The Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) system has identified famine conditions in several areas of North Darfur and the eastern Nuba Mountains, warning that the situation is expected to worsen further during the lean season, from July to October, in conflict zones where humanitarian access remains limited.

ODL/ac/Sf/APA

a6522.t:
The surprise attack by Hamas militants on Israel and some of its military installations has resulted in a declaration of war on Palestine, particularly the Gaza strip controlled by Hamas.
More than 1,300 people have been killed as Israel pummels Gaza, and battles continue between Hamas fighters and Israeli soldiers.
